💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Association of Photographers (AOP) has announced the 36 finalists for its 2026 AOP Open Awards, a competition celebrating still and moving images by professional and amateur photographers from around the world.
  • According to recent reports, now in its 20th year, the competition allows photographers of all experience levels to compete on equal terms.
  • Sources indicate that the finalists’ work will be exhibited at Fujifilm House of Photography in London from January 29 to March 14, 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Association of Photographers (AOP) has announced the 36 finalists for its 2026 AOP Open Awards, a competition celebrating still and moving images by professional and amateur photographers from around the world.

According to recent reports, now in its 20th year, the competition allows photographers of all experience levels to compete on equal terms. Sponsored by Capture One, Fujifilm UK, and Maxima, this year’s awards are divided into three formats: single image, series, and moving image.

Sources indicate that the finalists’ work will be exhibited at Fujifilm House of Photography in London from January 29 to March 14, 2027. The Gold and Silver winners will be announced at a private viewing on the evening of January 28.

The Best in Show winner will receive £1,250 ($1,600), while the Gold and Silver winners will take home £250 and £100, respectively. Additional prizes from the sponsors and AOP membership are also on offer.

The 36 shortlisted works cover a wide range of subjects, from LGBTIQ+ communities in the remote jungles of Suriname to Muslim women competing in Tbourida, an equestrian sport with roots in 16th-century battle tactics.

In a recent development, other projects explore the tradition of workers, local clubs, and Sunday league teams playing football on London’s Hackney Marshes, alongside images of the game being played away from conventional pitches in Morocco. Elsewhere, photographers document the 40,000 Elvis impersonators and fans who descend on Porthcawl, a small seaside town in South Wales, for the world’s largest Elvis Presley festival.

The finalists also include a portrait of a woman continuing to run her family’s flower business in Kyiv throughout the war in Ukraine, portraits of national treasures David Hockney and Dame Judi Dench, and a visual ode to gratitude for skin.

All 36 finalist projects can be viewed on the AOP Awards website.

Sources indicate that the AOP Open Awards accept entries without categories or prescribed themes, leaving photographers free to submit work that is either personal or commissioned. The competition welcomes still photography, moving images, and creative uses of technology and innovation in work produced by a person. AI-generated images are not accepted, and all entries must have been created on or after January 1, 2025.

Artists should receive tax breaks for donating their own work to UK museums, notes new philanthropy report

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a new report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.
  • The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a new report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.

The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.

The funding environment for culture has changed fundamentally, argues CPU which adds that “public finances have tightened considerably over the last 15 years, government funding for the arts has declined and self-generated income, while a key area, has not succeeded in plugging the widening gap.”.

In a wide-ranging set of recommendations, the report also suggests establishing a King’s Philanthropy Medal for Culture and setting up a national cultural “match-and-seed funding” programme with a regional focus.

Recent findings suggest that alison Cole, the director of the CPU and former editor of The Art Newspaper, says: “While the arts funding environment has changed dramatically in recent years, the philanthropic landscape has hardly kept pace let alone filled the gap with the UK lagging far behind the incentives offered by many of our European and US counterparts. We need a new national strategy that not only identifies the opportunities and need, but also thrives on a spirit of creative collaboration and mutual respect.”.

Artists who donate their own works to qualifying cultural institutions should receive tax recognition based on independent valuation, states the think tank. Other tax-based recommendations include protecting charitable giving through inheritance planning—which means simplifying inheritance tax rules—and providing clearer rules around VAT.

Charles Saumarez Smith, who previously led the National Gallery, National Portrait Gallery and the Royal Academy of Arts, told The Art Newspaper that the report is “sensible”. “I particularly appreciated the information as to how other countries encourage philanthropy, not just the US,” he claims. “The biggest matter seems to me to be the lack of clarity round the existing systems, including, for example, around inheritance. How many people, even within cultural institutions, knows how this operates?”.

Industry observers note that the CPU acknowledges that Britain has a strong philanthropic tradition, arguing that its potential for cultural giving remains unrealised. Gift Aid, Acceptance in Lieu and the Cultural Gifts Scheme have all delivered real benefits but these schemes should be enhanced so that donors are more aware of their benefits, the report says.

It has been revealed that UK incentives are “broadly generous, but they are structured very differently from overseas models,“ according to the report. “The practical result is that British donors give quietly and anonymously, while the US and other systems reward public foundations and naming opportunities.”.

Kate Rolfe, a cultural strategy consultant, states: "Art organisations need to work with philanthropists who are inspired by the organisational vision and share their values and priorities, ensuring that the museum can stay focused on its purpose, vision and audiences." She believes corporate donations need to be reincentivised, as these often "lead to really creative partnerships based on shared audiences and values". Rolfe founded The Revels Office, a strategic audience and commercial development consultancy for the culture sector.

“Focused giving” may be partly the answer claims the CPU, as evidenced by the Domani project at the National Gallery in London with £375m secured from Crankstart, the charitable foundation of Sir Michael Moritz and his wife Harriet Heyman, and the Julia Rausing Trust for a latest Modern art wing. “The real transformation needs to be across the country and not just in the capital,” adds Cole.

MoMA to Host First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Over 20 Years

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The indelible impact of late Cuban-American artist Ana Mendieta's practice will be celebrated in a forthcoming retrospective in Fresh York next year.
  • MoMA's announcement comes just two months before Tate Modern's ongoing Mendieta retrospective closes in London.
  • Born in Cuba and raised in Iowa from age 12 as a child evacuee through Operation Peter Pan, Mendieta ruminated on themes of displacement, ancestral memory, ecology, and the politics of the female body, as well as its connection with the natural world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The indelible impact of late Cuban-American artist Ana Mendieta's practice will be celebrated in a forthcoming retrospective in Fresh York next year. Scheduled to open at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in Manhattan in December 2027, Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective marks the first presentation of Mendieta's overarching career in the United States in over 20 years.

MoMA's announcement comes just two months before Tate Modern's ongoing Mendieta retrospective closes in London. Comprising around 200 works, including rarely seen formative drawings and newly remastered films, the MoMA exhibition will present Mendieta's artistic process, signature developments, and career milestones in a chronological fashion. Starting with early figurative works completed during her undergraduate and graduate studies at the University of Iowa, the exhibition will follow the artist's subsequent expansion in making and documenting her performance art, as well as her foray into sculpture, installation, and site-specific land art.

Born in Cuba and raised in Iowa from age 12 as a child evacuee through Operation Peter Pan, Mendieta ruminated on themes of displacement, ancestral memory, ecology, and the politics of the female body, as well as its connection with the natural world. She's best known for her Silueta (1973–80) series, in which the outline of her body (either present or absent) is embedded, extruded, burned, or embellished into various natural environments as a physical and spiritual reunion with the earth. These “earth-body works,” as Mendieta called them, dealt with Mesoamerican and Afro-Caribbean divinity, natural reclamation and life cycles, and the deconstruction of borders.

Recent findings suggest that presaging Mendieta's groundbreaking Siluetas were transgressive performance pieces centering the use of blood as a signifier of violence, fertility, vitality, and ancestral ritual. Her 1973 performance “Untitled (Rape Scene)” and its photo documentation were created in response to the rape and murder of 20-year-old University of Iowa student Sarah Ann Ottens, whereas her filmed performance of “Untitled (Death of a Chicken)” (1972) graphically referenced animal sacrifice practices associated with Santería.

The retrospective also centers the artist's lens-based work, her sustained interest in organic material, and how her travels, reunion with Cuba, and art residencies sparked major evolutions in her practice. Mendieta's 1981 Esculturas Rupestres (Rupestrian Sculptures) series, 1983–85 fellowship at the American Academy in Rome, and a variety of later works, including a series of ink-wash drawings, are among the highlights mentioned by the museum.

According to recent reports, “Ana Mendieta rigorously investigated the physical, conceptual, and emotional potential of materials like soil, sand, water, blood, leaves, wood, and fire to create images that speak across time and geography,” said Beverly Adams, MoMA's Latin American art curator and retrospective co-organizer, in a press statement. “In doing so, she redefined the boundaries between sculpture and action, object and image, and private and public.”.

In celebrating Mendieta's punctuated career, the retrospective apparently strays away from the tragic circumstances of the 36-year-old artist's death and the unshakeable speculations that continue to follow. Such is the case with Mendieta's ongoing exhibition at the Tate Modern, which also omitted mentioning the artist's death and the resulting controversy surrounding her husband, artist Carl Andre.

Nevertheless, the artist's own poignant grapplings with loss and rebirth are staged independently of the discourse, underscoring her persisting critical impact in a visual arts landscape that has rarely offered credit to women artists.

Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective will be on view at MoMA from December 12, 2027 to April 15, 2028.

No rounded cards or drop shadows get in the way, so the web design reads cleanly on a single scan.

In Memoriam honors those we recently lost in the art world.

Arpita Singh (1937–2026)Indian painter who bridged fantasy and reality.

One of the most high-profile contemporary Indian artists, Singh fused violent realism and fantasy imagery, constantly innovating across a six-decade career. In the 1970s and '80s, for instance, she explored abstraction, producing spare compositions filled with dots and dashes. She became more widely known in the West due to an exhibition at Serpentine Galleries just last year.

"Singh never settles into a mode or style," critic John Yau wrote in a 2017 review of her exhibition at Fresh Delhi- and New York-based Talwar Gallery for this magazine. "This body of work, which is being shown for the first time in America, is a singular achievement.".

Stedelijk Museum appoints Krist Gruijthuijsen as newly introduced director

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (396 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has announced that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its latest director from July 2027.
  • Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he stated he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.
  • According to recent reports, “The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has announced that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its latest director from July 2027.

Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he stated he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.

According to recent reports, “The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “People go to the Rijksmuseum for Rembrandt and to the city [Stedelijk] museum to understand how Amsterdam has developed, to understand Modernism through the lens of art and design.”.

In a recent development, the Stedelijk Museum enjoyed success last year with an Anselm Kiefer show—organised with the neighbouring Van Gogh Museum—and an exhibition of work by the Dutch photographer Erwin Olaf, increasing annual ticket revenue compared to 2024 by almost a quarter, to €10.8 million. Its current Yayoi Kusama show has been extended to the end of January due to its popularity.

Sources indicate that this success stands out against a backdrop of Dutch museums reporting financial pressure and a fall in visits compared to pre-pandemic levels. The Rijksmuseum’s most recent annual report describes internal discussions that took place about the fact visitor numbers fell 4% in 2025 to 2.3 million, while the Rembrandt House Museum recently warned that rising tourist taxes will damage cultural tourism.

But Gruijthuijsen said he is more interested in variety than visitor records. “I’m not a visitor numbers director,” he indicates. “It is quality rather than quantity: what we need economically, and the rest is a plus. It is very difficult these days because people only choose what they know. My goal is first and foremost to support artists and art.”.

Gruijthuijsen takes over from Rein Wolfs, who has been the director since 2019.

From one of the first exhibitions to establish Van Gogh’s work in 1905 to experimental reveals of the 1960s, the Stedelijk Museum created an international reputation for contemporary art, which Gruijthuijsen wants to make relevant today. “The DNA of the city museum is a modern day and global perspective—trying to find connections,” he states.

From the Finns, he will also bring an key lesson in terms of improving diversity and tackling under-represented subjects, he states: “Less talking, more doing.”.

  • Indulgence is in the air right now, and not just because we’re closing in on Thanksgiving weekend.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My mom called me greedy in jest this weekend because I had the gall to eat … more than five (but fewer than 10!) square slices of a delicious ube cake in her presence. Unlike each savored bite of that addictive purple pastry, I took her criticism on the chin because I believe that greed and indulgence function as a Venn diagram rather than as synonyms. And because there was still plenty of cake to go around.

Indulgence is in the air right now, and not just because we’re closing in on Thanksgiving weekend. Marquee auctions have rolled in like a thick fog on Monday, not long after the ADAA fair and an adjunctive torrential downpour rinsed the last of art fair season out of New York late last week. A press release from Sotheby’s informed me that $1.1 billion worth of art will go under the hammer this month, underpinned by today’s sale of a rarely seen van Gogh landscape expected to fetch a record-breaking $180 million. A brief shakeup ensued less than a week before the painting goes to auction, as the descendants of its former owner suddenly called on Sotheby’s to withdraw the work, alleging that it was sold under duress due to Nazi persecution.

Don’t worry, though — the auction house shared in a follow-up release that the descendants and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, who are selling the painting alongside 11 other multimillion-dollar masterpieces from their collection, have come to a “mutually satisfactory resolution” that allows the sale to proceed as scheduled.

Really glad they worked that out.

Industry observers note that on the other side of the same coin, protesters gathered outside of the Museum of Modern Art during an annual benefit for the museum’s Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center last Thursday, calling on filmmaker and honored guest Steven Spielberg to reject the recognition and boycott the museum over Leon Black’s Epstein-related sexual abuse allegations. Cold, biting rain soaked the group of 20 artists and activists outside the gala, and Spielberg hasn’t acknowledged their demands.

In a recent development, all things considered, Iraqi-British data journalist and illustrator Mona Chalabi’s first-ever book, which was released last week, comes at a most opportune time. The book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026), comes from Chalabi five-year endeavor in examining class inequality in the United States by analyzing the incomes, expenses, tax deductions, systemic barriers, and livelihoods of 10 Americans across the nation. In a recent interview with Hyperallergic’s Lakshmi Rivera Amin, Chalabi noted that journalists themselves often don’t acknowledge or even recognize how their own class upbringing can color their reporting on wealth and poverty, whereas other markers like race and gender are positioned as lenses of understanding.

Sources indicate that A new video exhibition on the High Line also tackles greed and indulgence through the lens of the British Empire’s storied trade monopolies and resource theft across South Asia and China. Works by Shahzia Sikander and the artist duo Hylozoic/Desires unpack the British stronghold on salt in India and the empire’s deliberate opium influx in China during the Qing dynasty, while also highlighting historic and speculative subversions that disrupt dominant colonial narratives.

Recent findings suggest that I wasn’t super fond of the High Line’s most recent film installation, but this one sounds more up my alley on a subjective, personal history level. I’m looking forward to checking it out soon — before the weather really turns south — and visiting the Mighty Miniatures exhibition that’s opening this Saturday at the National Museum of the American Indian.

Breaking: Is My Art Funny to You?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare.
  • According to recent reports, what to make of art that makes us laugh?
  • Humor is “an emotional response that’s a little bit like a sneak attack,” Brown stated in an interview with Hyperallergic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare. Called “Duchenne laughter” after a 19th-century neurologist, the gesture is bodily, sometimes to a repulsive degree. But most of the time, we laugh because we feel that we should — that it would behoove us socially. In a talk at the Aspen AIR Festival this year, poet and psychoanalyst Nuar Alsadir described eliciting Duchenne laughter as an attempt “to strip away the layers of socialization and the false self.” While laughter “flies under the radar because of our associations to it as being joyful,” when you dig deeper, it’s “usually coming from some kind of conflict in the unconscious.”.

According to recent reports, what to make of art that makes us laugh? (Or at least desperately wants to?) Does This Taste Funny?: Humor in Contemporary Art, a sprawling exhibition across at Lehman College Art Gallery in the Bronx and The Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence in Bronxville, proposes comedy as a potent artistic device. Co-curators Melissa Brown, artist and professor of art at Lehman College, and John O’Connor, artist and chair of the Visual and Studio Arts program at Sarah Lawrence, use humor’s various tones — absurd, cringe, slapstick, ironic — as organizing principles to present the work of 41 artists. From museum-collection heavy hitters like Ray Johnson and Cindy Sherman, to established cartoonists Roz Chast and Aline Kominsky-Crumb, to contemporary rising stars such as Ebecho Muslimova, Does This Taste Funny? implores us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.

Humor is “an emotional response that’s a little bit like a sneak attack,” Brown stated in an interview with Hyperallergic. “It causes you to think about things in a way that is not led by a press release, not predetermined by art history. There’s something that’s very, very personal about it.” Indeed, humor tends to be anti-didactic. You either guffaw or giggle, or you don’t. Alsadir would say that what you find funny or not provides information about your psychic state — what does it say about me that I chuckled sympathetically at Jill Danenberg’s 2024 accordion book Underground Comic, detailing trials and tribulations between veganism and feminism, while my mouth refused to curl for Tony Matelli’s “Veg Man” (2008), a droopily vegetal bronze figure?

The participatory nature of humor means this show is uniquely invested in perception, and in provoking a certain response. As at an open mic, I felt the pressure of bearing witness, aware of my role as an audience member with the power to deem certain works successful or not by producing that ever-elusive involuntary laugh. This semester, O’Connor is teaching an undergraduate class on taking laughter seriously: He tasked his students with making small sculptures, their only instruction to try to be “the funniest in the class.” The winning piece, according to votes cast via smiley-face stickers on a table outside the gallery, is a realistic bust of Professor O’Connor with a No. 2 pencil stuck halfway up his nose. Second place was a reference to a meme O’Connor still doesn’t quite understand.

According to recent reports, the oldest featured work in Does This Taste Funny? is Karl Wirsum’s drawing “Untitled (Study for Blue Tattoo)” (1964), featuring a classic Sailor Jerry star design on the tongue of a woman sporting a perfect mid-century housewife hairdo. Getting the reference is crucial to appreciating a good joke beyond the most base level of someone farting or slipping on a banana peel (which, to get psychoanalytic again, we laugh at to mask our own shame). Brown and O’Connor’s curation is never insidery or niche to the canon, but they are aware of the quality of funniness changing over time.

Some of O’Connor’s students recognized River Phoenix in Ray Johnson’s mail-art collage; more were taken by Jeremy Couillard’s “Escape from Lavender Island” (2023), an open-world video game simulation featuring deep-fried animation aesthetics and relatably tragic dialogue from the depths of neoliberal hell (“While he ate he would watch film classics on an overpriced streaming service and sometimes cry.”).

It has been revealed that “Absurdism ends up being pretty timeless,” Brown remarked. “Using ridiculously absurd materials to make work that doesn’t connect necessarily to a political moment or a socioeconomic concern, it represents this irreverent attitude towards art-making.” And apparently that’s what appeals to Gen Z, who are inundated with visual content, yet perhaps still seeking a response to contemporary life that truly resonates.

Brown, who has been teaching at Lehman for 20 years, wants artists to find their idiosyncratic voice. If being funny comes naturally, maybe that’s the tack they should take.

Industry observers note that “There’s such a tendency for imitation out there. You can easily become a version of something that exists, and that is no longer considered a bad thing,” she said. “I'm interested in trying to find, ‘What's your really weird way of approaching that?’”.

Take Kristen Mills’s “It IS Cake” (2026), a filmic parody of the Netflix baking contest series Is It Cake? using entirely brown cardboard, displayed in the gallery on a screen within a faux kitchen made of the same plainly bland material. Installed nearby is puppet theater ephemera that does directly respond to a political moment: John Vasquez Mejias’s “The Puerto Rican War” (2026), which expands his novelette about revolutionaries fighting colonialism in 1950. The Puerto Ricans’ demands aren’t funny, but some of the depictions of American incompetence are.

Does This Taste Funny? reminds us of humor as a tool, as a way to frame whatever it is that we hope to communicate. Life is not always joyful, but it should at least be emotional. At Sarah Lawrence, I watched Robert DeJesus’s surreal video “The Survey” (2024), starring a talking Olmec head who speaks only when there are no corroborative witnesses. I didn’t laugh. Later in the day, turning a corner on the grounds of Lehman College, I was suddenly confronted with the stone statue, whose onscreen lips I’d just seen move. I audibly snorted.

Welcome to our roundup of daily art news, featuring top stories and timely updates handpicked by Hyperallergic’s writers and editors. Have a news tip? Get in touch with us.

Georgia O’Keeffe’s “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” (1930), which was rediscovered in the back of an East Village closet where it was stored for four decades, fetched $4.9 million at Christie’s 20th-Century Evening Sale last night, November 18, surpassing its $2-3 estimate. Read Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar’s report detailing the fascinating backstory behind the painting, created just one year after the artist's first visit to New Mexico.

Days before the close of this year’s Venice Biennale, 10 European Union countries are demanding that the European Commission exclude Russia from the 2027 architecture biennale. “In light of the current geopolitical realities … there should be no room for ‘normalisation’ of Russia’s participation in international sporting and cultural events, as long as there is no just and lasting peace in Ukraine,” reads a letter signed by representatives in Poland, Austria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden, according to Rapporteur.

Ahead of its 50th anniversary next year, Public Art Fund has declared its 2027 exhibition program. The organization will continue its longstanding bus shelter series with I Happen to Like New York, which will transform 700 JCDecaux shelters across New York, Chicago, and Boston with the works of 19 artists, including Nicole Eisenman, Louis Fratino, and Toyin Ojih Odutola. New outdoor public sculptures from Ugo Rondinone, Lotus Kang, and Firelei Báez, a photo series from Catherine Opie, and a first-of-its-kind participatory performance by Jeremy Dweller round out Public Art Fund's 2027 offerings.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.

“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, said at the end of the evening.

Heffel's evening auctions in Toronto on 18 November Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

Sources indicate that the back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).

In a recent development, hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.

Emily Carr, Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure), around 1912 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

Industry observers note that the second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.

Industry observers note that A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).

Jean Paul Riopelle, Herbeuse, 1967 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.

Sources indicate that among the night’s other big-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.

Paul-Émile Borduas, Empâtement, 1957 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.

Arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a upcoming auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.

Ivan Eyre, Golden Rod, 1981 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

It has been revealed that cash Price: A quick search on Google Flights confirms what you suspected — this itinerary in business class retails for approximately $8,000 per person during the shoulder season. During the Australian summer or holiday periods, it climbs closer to $11,000–$12,000.

Your Cost: 55,000 Alaska Mileage Strategy miles + approximately $85 in taxes and fees. Per person.

Industry observers note that CPP Calculation: At $8,000 cash value, your 55,000 miles are worth 14.5 cents per point — more than seven times what you'd get redeeming Alaska miles for domestic economy. At $12,000, you're at 21.8 cents per point, which is among the highest CPP figures available anywhere in the U.S. loyalty ecosystem.

Cathay's 1-2-1 herringbone configuration means your suite sits at a slight angle, with a sliding privacy door, a true flat-bed (78 inches fully reclined), a large 18-inch entertainment screen, and a dedicated storage compartment for your belongings. After takeoff, a flight attendant takes your dinner order — think pan-seared duck breast or a selection of regional Hong Kong specialties. You sleep. You land refreshed.

Total cost for two: 110,000 Alaska miles + roughly $170 in fees. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: extraordinary experiences made nearly free through a system anyone can learn.

Sources indicate that alaska's booking window opens 331 days out. Cathay Pacific releases business class award space to partner programs in limited quantities, and the best dates disappear quickly. Set a calendar alert for 331 days before your target travel date and be ready to search — and call — that morning.

In a recent development, the single best technique for this redemption: run your search on ba.com before calling Alaska. BA's search engine is faster, more reliable for Cathay availability, and lets you visually scan a full month of dates. Identify two or three date options before you pick up the phone. This dramatically shortens your call time and reduces the chance of getting an agent who says "I'm not seeing anything.".

Don't treat the Hong Kong stopover as a layover — treat it as a destination. Alaska's routing rules explicitly allow a free stopover on one-way awards. Two to four nights in Hong Kong costs you nothing extra in miles. Pair this with a cheap positioning flight or use it as an anchor for a broader Asia itinerary.

Industry observers note that book two one-way redemptions rather than a round-trip. This gives you full flexibility on return routing — you might come back on Qantas through another city, or extend your trip without penalty.

Recent findings suggest that since there are no major flexible currency transfer paths into Alaska (no Chase, Amex, or Citi transfers), the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature from Bank of America is your most efficient earning vehicle. The welcome bonus alone can cover a significant portion of this redemption. Pair with everyday spending in categories that earn elevated miles.

If Cathay availability is closed on your dates, Qantas Business Class to Australia prices at the same 55,000 miles. This redemption is purpose-built for the FI-minded couple or solo traveler who is willing to invest some effort in the booking process in exchange for an extraordinary, nearly free experience. If you've been dreaming about Australia and refuse to pay $8,000–$12,000 for a business class ticket — but you're also not willing to spend 20+ hours crammed in economy for a trip this significant — this is your answer.

According to recent reports, minimum requirements: You need 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per person. For two travelers, that's 110,000 miles. If you're building from zero through the Alaska Visa, factor in 6–12 months of earning runway before booking.

In a recent development, this redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is honest. It's not complicated in concept, but it has two specific friction points that trip up even experienced travel rewards enthusiasts. **Challenge 1: Earning the Miles** Alaska Mileage Plan's isolation from major flexible currency programs (no Chase Ultimate Rewards, no Amex Membership Rewards, no Citi ThankYou transfers directly) means you can't simply funnel points you already have into Alaska. The primary path is the Alaska Airlines Visa (Bank of America) or a Marriott Bonvoy conversion at an unfavorable 3:1 ratio. The call-in process intimidates people who've only ever booked travel digitally. **Tip:** Do your homework on ba.com first, have your dates ready, and approach the call as an informed customer — not someone asking for help finding availability. Agents respond well to specific, prepared callers. **Challenge 3: Cathay Award Availability** Cathay Pacific releases partner award space selectively and often in small quantities. Availability rated 3/5. **Tip:** Search exactly at the 331-day booking window, keep Qantas as your backup at the same price point, and be flexible with travel dates by even one or two days — a Tuesday departure often has inventory when Saturday doesn't. The good news: once you've done this once, you'll understand the system deeply enough to replicate it. The ChooseFI community has members who've booked this exact route multiple times. The first time takes effort. After that, it's a process you know cold.

The fastest path is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card from Bank of America, which typically offers a 60,000 to 75,000-mile sign-up bonus. That alone nearly covers the 55,000 miles needed. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy points at 3:1 (165,000 Bonvoy points equals 55,000 Alaska miles) or earn miles through flying Alaska and its partners.

Cathay Pacific typically releases Business Class award space 90 to 330 days before departure. The sweet spot for finding availability is usually 90 to 120 days out, when airlines release unsold premium cabin seats. Check frequently, as availability can appear and disappear quickly.

Sources indicate that alaska allows one free stopover on one-way awards. On a routing from the US to Australia via Hong Kong, you can stop in Hong Kong for any number of days at no additional miles cost. Simply tell the agent when booking that you want a stopover in HKG. This effectively gives you two destinations for the price of one redemption.

The Alaska Mileage Strategy redemption for Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class to Australia is one of the most extraordinary sweet spots in travel rewards. At 55,000 miles for a seat that costs $5,000 to $12,000 in cash — with zero fuel surcharges and a free stopover in Hong Kong — this redemption delivers 9 to 22 cents per point. It requires more planning and effort than a simple hotel booking, but the payoff is a genuine luxury travel experience that proves the asymmetric value the FI community builds its travel rewards strategy around.

It has been revealed that for decades, the word “Palestinian” conjured a very specific image in the minds of many intellectuals and members of the public: the commanding presence of Edward Noted, credited with no less than revolutionizing our collective understanding of the dynamics of oppression. Breaking: Iconic and Independent: New York Studio School's MFA Program

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (479 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What does it mean to give art the time and attention it requires?
  • Located at 8 West 8th Street in Greenwich Village, the School occupies a building with a rich history in American art.
  • The School’s full-time, two-year Master of Fine Arts (MFA) program is a 60-credit degree centered on intensive, individual studio practice in drawing, painting, sculpture, and art history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What does it mean to give art the time and attention it requires? Since its founding in 1964, the New York Studio School (NYSS) has pursued this question through an approach to art education grounded in sustained studio practice, rigorous inquiry, and the conviction that artists develop through the ongoing process of making, looking, and thinking.

Located at 8 West 8th Street in Greenwich Village, the School occupies a building with a rich history in American art. Founded by artist and educator Mercedes Matter, NYSS carries forward a tradition of independent thinking and experimentation, offering an environment where artists can challenge assumptions, investigate fundamental questions, and develop their work through direct engagement with materials and ideas.

The School’s full-time, two-year Master of Fine Arts (MFA) program is a 60-credit degree centered on intensive, individual studio practice in drawing, painting, sculpture, and art history. Rather than prescribing a single artistic direction, the program provides students with the time, space, and mentorship to pursue their own questions and cultivate their own distinctive artistic language.

At the heart of the Fresh York Studio School MFA program is the relationship between individual practice and collective exchange. Students are assigned private or semi-private studio spaces and select two core faculty artists to serve as their atelier mentors. Through studio visits, group critiques, and ongoing dialogue with faculty and peers, students are encouraged to examine their work from multiple perspectives while developing the confidence and critical awareness to move their practice forward.

The curriculum combines independent studio work with intensive two-week Marathons, drawing courses, Critical Studies seminars, and encounters with visiting artists. The School’s renowned Evening Lecture Series and Exhibitions further connect students to a broad community of artists, writers, historians, and thinkers. Drawing remains a foundational component of the program, informing the study of painting and sculpture and encouraging deeper attention to perception, form, space, and material.

Students in the MFA program are encouraged to engage with the histories of art while questioning established conventions, exploring the relationships between representation and abstraction, and discovering fresh possibilities through sustained experimentation. The goal is to support the development of an independent, thoughtful, and resilient artistic practice. The MFA program’s second year culminates with a thesis project and exhibition in the School’s historic galleries, connecting a new generation of artists with a building that has been part of New York’s cultural life for more than a century.

For artists seeking a demanding, immersive environment in which to deepen their work, the Newly introduced York Studio School offers an education built around the essential questions of art-making, and the time, community, and commitment needed to pursue them.

Recent findings suggest that applications are now open for Fall 2027 admission. For full consideration for admission and financial aid, apply by the Priority Deadline: January 15.

Learn more about the MFA program and apply at nyss.org.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1663 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in New York

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in New York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees).
  • Industry observers note that just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%.
  • Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in New York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.

Industry observers note that just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.

Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.

Another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.

Andy Warhol, Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), 1962 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.

Still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a new home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).

In a recent development, A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.

The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of key 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.

It has been revealed that illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.

Vija Celmins, Untitled (Ocean), 1990 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

According to recent reports, gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in New York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.

Gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in New York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.

A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).

Jim Nutt, Loom, 1999 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Sources indicate that A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a fresh auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.

Though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.

Alice Neel, David and Catherine Saalfield, 1982 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

According to recent reports, the appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime Fresh York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.).

It has been revealed that among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s New York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.

Large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.

The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.

Jean-Michel Basquiat, Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), 1983 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.

Measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and important champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.

Julia Jo, One Fell Swoop, 2026 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

In a recent development, the evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the New York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.).

According to recent reports, apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca stated. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”.

The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

Sometime in the 1980s, when I was still a fledgling curator of 20th-century art at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, I was invited to the studio of a rather prominent artist. During our conversation, the work of Jacob Lawrence came up somehow, and the artist mentioned that he was impressed by what he described as Lawrence’s use of “Black” colors. Did I mention this artist was White?

Sources indicate that I was gobsmacked by the comment. Not that I wasn’t attuned to stereotypical societal associations of color — most notably, of bright, loud colors with Black people. In the 1950s, a full three decades before Nancy Reagan practically made red her official color, my Aunt Ruth was appalled that my mother made red coats for my sister and me, rather than using more acceptable pastel colors. Then a friend who grew up in Northern Ireland told me that Protestant Irish factions associated Catholic Irish with loud and bright colors.

But how did such racially associative ideas translate to the realm of the so-called “fine” arts? I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of vital theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026).

In a recent development, the Walker Youngbird Foundation named Native artist Dustin Newman (Unangax̂/Deg Hit’an Athabascan) the annual recipient of its Núhi grant today, November 19. The Alaskan artist will use the $10,000 award to revive and pass down the endangered craftsmanship behind qayaatx̂ux, traditional closed crown visors worn by Unangax̂ chiefs.

It has been revealed that through technical research with the Anchorage Museum and collaborations with regional hat-makers, Newman will produce a small series of visors to gift to cultural leaders. An intricately decorated hunting hat historically worn by chiefs and high-ranking whaling captains, the qayaatx̂ux began fading into obscurity in the early 20th century due to factors including American colonization. After completing the series, Newman will share the tradition with community members through Camp Qungaayux on the island of Unalaska and the Agdaagux Culture Camp in King Cove, the fishing village where the artist was raised.

"I first started bending visors at 17 with my mentor Okalena Patricia Lekanoff-Gregory at our regional culture camp in Anchorage and Unalaska," Newman told Hyperallergic. "Why I chose to pursue this project through the Núhi Grant was to uplift the status of these visors not as a wall hanging but as a symbol within our communities honoring our culture bearers and community leaders.".

The Raptor Pro Max has 42 cross blue laser lines, up from 22 on the Raptor Pro, and it can reach up to 1.26 million measurements, raising the maximum scanning rate by approximately 91% while offering a single capture range of up to 480 × 330 mm at a working distance of 550 mm.

It has been revealed that that wider coverage and higher scanning rate mean that you can capture more of a bumper, door or body panel in each pass, which gives successive frames more shared geometry to maintain stable tracking. The expanded coverage also helps reduce the number of markers required by up to 25%.

According to recent reports, creality indicates the reduction of repeat passes, the need for repositioning and the application of markers means consumers can complete scans of automotive workpieces in up to 40% less time. That will allow custom parts to be moved into design and trial-fitting work more promptly.

Sources indicate that for smaller features, there's also the option to switch to seven parallel blue laser lines to capture edges, threads, and chamfers. Together, the two blue laser modes cover objects from 5 to 4,000 mm in size. Creality cites volumetric accuracy of 0.02 mm + 0.08 mm/m.² The blue lasers can also capture suitable black and metallic surfaces without scanning spray.

During handheld scanning, real-time preview in Creality Scan lets operators monitor coverage as they move around a part. The Blue Laser Line Mode operates at up to 60 fps and the a near-infrared (NIR) structured-light mode at up to 30 fps, with geometry or texture tracking. There's built-in anti-shake functionality to help reduce the impact of hand movement.

The Creality Raptor Pro Max has a suggested retail price of $1,799, which is reduced by around 10% for a limited time to $1,619. There's also a limited-time bundle including a Scan Bridge for $1,799.

This month, a Las Vegas man pled guilty to a felony violation of the Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 after being charged with selling counterfeit Native American art misrepresented as authentic to consumers. A United States district court judge for Nevada sentenced Jose Martinez, who adopted the name Joseph Skywolf, to two years of supervised probation and court-ordered restitution for the infraction.

Sources indicate that A release from the US Department of the Interior's Indian Arts and Crafts Board (IACB) outlined that Martinez falsely claimed to be Chiricahua Apache, Apache, Navajo, and Native American while promoting his mobile business Skywolf's Gallery. Through the business, which was once headquartered in Jackson, Wyoming, but traveled to venues and markets across the Great Plains and Southwest, Martinez deliberately sold counterfeit artwork and handicrafts, including headdresses, jewelry, paintings, and beaded tanned hides falsely attributed to Native artists or specific tribes.

Last summer, Martinez was indicted on one count of violating the Indian Arts and Crafts Act, which prohibits the sale of products falsely marketed as authentic American Indian or Alaska Native art and craftwork. The act is intended to protect the livelihoods, cultural knowledge, and artistic traditions of recognized Native tribes, bands, and communities, as well as consumers seeking authentic cultural heritage and art objects.

Five Ethiopian artefacts restituted in London ceremony

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November).
  • In a recent development, mcCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art.
  • Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November). The process was part of a wider initiative by the American collector Robert McCarthy and the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio that is expected to see many more objects returned to Ethiopia.

In a recent development, mcCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art. He broadened his collection in the 1990s to include Ethiopian art, at a time when there was less concern about provenance. In 2023-24 he lent objects to the exhibition Ethiopia at the Crossroads, which was presented in venues in Baltimore, Salem in Massachusetts and Toledo. It was at Toledo that he began discussions with Sophie Ong, assistant director of strategic initiatives, about the future of his collection.

Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

This eventually led to the new, complex arrangement. Toledo will acquire McCarthy’s 375 Ethiopian objects, one of the largest such private collections. Two thirds will be donated and the remainder bought. Some of this material will be exhibited when the museum’s galleries reopen in autumn 2027 after a major reinstallation of its permanent collection.

According to recent reports, the museum then intends to return much of the collection to Ethiopia, in tranches over the next 20 years. Any items deemed to have left Ethiopia illegally or inappropriately will be restituted. Details have not been released, but it is assumed that this will include looted material seized by British troops at the 1869 battle of Maqdala and which later came onto the international art market.

According to recent reports, objects judged to have been exported properly will remain at the Toledo museum. Stewardship of items with an indeterminate status will be decided jointly by the Toledo museum and Ethiopian officials. It is thought that ultimately half of McCarthy’s 375 items may be returned.

Industry observers note that the unusual tripartite arrangement between McCarthy, the Toledo museum and the Ethiopia authorities could prove to be a template for dealing with restitution claims by other African countries. At the handover, Alula Pankhurst, speaking on behalf of the Ethiopian Heritage Authority, described it as “a new model of partnership”.

Recent findings suggest that this week’s restitution of five objects to the government’s Ethiopian Heritage Authority is slightly different, in that they have been directly returned by McCarthy. The Toledo museum was unwilling to accession them because of records suggesting that they had left Ethiopia after the 1970 Unesco convention.

The items are two 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and three processional crosses. All are believed to have been improperly removed from Ethiopian churches.

In a recent development, the earliest of the two manuscripts is a Book of Revelation with a Horologium (daily cycle of prayers). It includes seven full-page illuminations, dating from around 1400. The volume was recorded in the late 20th century as being in the Saqqā Madḫānē Ālam Church in Šawā Province.

It has been revealed that the other manuscript is a large mid-15th century Gospels, which includes full-page images of the Four Evangelists. The scholar Diana Spencer noted in a 1974 article that she saw it at the church of Emmaus Giyor near Wafa Yasus.

Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

The three brass processional crosses being returned date variously from the late-18th to early-20th centuries. Each has incised inscriptions which may make it possible to determine which church they came from.

In a recent development, the five returned objects are now being sent from London to the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa, where a new display of restituted material is scheduled to open in December. Most of the rest of the display will be material which had been looted at Maqdala.

However, the forthcoming Addis Ababa display may feed into a debate over whether religious items that can be identified with a particular location should be retained in the National Museum or returned to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

GTA VI trendjacking was already everywhere, even before today's release of the most- anticipated video game in history (see our GTA VI review for our Digital Art Editor's experience playing it). A lot of the attempts to jump on the bandwagon have been lazy and half-hearted, with brands merely using AI image generators to give product shots a vaporwave makeover.

Industry observers note that the optical chain Specsavers has turned out to be an unlikely exception. Its unusual GTA VI campaign might actually be the best brand collaboration of the year.

A post shared by Specsavers (@specsavers).

That's right, Specsavers has entered into its "biggest partnership of all time’. It's sponsoring GTA... just not that GTA.

According to recent reports, the teaser post above might have raised eyebrows among gamers given that GTA VI developer and publisher Rockstar Games has very limited collaborations. There's it's deal with the Miami Heat (and with Oakley for the GTA VI Collector's Edition), but there are only parody fake brands in GTA VI itself.

Industry observers note that but Specsavers isn't sponsoring the video game that everyone's talking about. It's hooked up with GTA Transport Ltd, a British road haulage firm based in Leicester. Which sounds a bit like Leonida, right?

“It might not be the GTA partnership I originally had in mind but a deal’s a deal. I'm pleased to offer every driver at GTA Transport a free eye test,” the tech giant's brand partnerships and sponsorships lead Neil Liddle said.

Bugz Singh from GTA Transport Ltd mentioned: “We were surprised when Specsavers got in touch, but we’re delighted to be the GTA they’ve teamed up with. Our drivers spend all day on the road, so they’re looking forward to their eye tests.”.

A post shared by Specsavers (@specsavers).

Specsavers' stunt rises above most of the GTA VI trendjacking that we've seen. It's funny, and it's a lot more creative and memorable than simply throwing Vice City hues onto brand imagery. Best of all, it indicates that Specsavers really knows its brand and its public, maintaining consistency with the message it's been using for over 20 years.

Industry observers note that specsavers has been telling the same joke since 2002, and it still works. In fact, it's become even more effective. The line 'Should've gone to Specsavers', coined by then in-house creative director Graham Daldry, is now so ingrained in the public consciousness that it no longer needs to be appended onto the campaign. It's already implied.

In a recent development, having already sold close to 16 million copies before today's release, GTA VI is a cultural phenomenon with a reach that extends well beyond that of most games. An AI-generated vaporwave graphic can't make an unrelated brand a part of that, but Specsavers has shown that on-brand creative thinking can forge a memorable connection to the entertainment event of the year.

Latest Update: Hyatt Luxury — Park Hyatt for 25,000-30,000 Points

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • Imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji.
  • The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt New York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

According to recent reports, here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating**, and it's worth being specific about where the friction lives — because once you understand it, most of the difficulty evaporates. **The earning is easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards points flow into World of Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, and Chase is one of the most accessible premium rewards ecosystems for fresh-to-intermediate travel rewards participants. This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Plan further ahead than feels natural. If you want Tokyo in April of next year, you should be searching in late March or early April of the current year. 2. **Be flexible by 3–5 days on either side.** Award inventory often opens mid-week when demand is lower. Shifting from a Saturday check-in to a Thursday can unlock availability that doesn't exist on peak nights. 3. **Check repeatedly near the 30-day mark.** Properties occasionally release additional award space as the date approaches. Setting a weekly reminder to re-check your target dates costs nothing. If you're willing to plan ahead and stay flexible on exact dates, moderate difficulty becomes very manageable — and the reward on the other side is worth every bit of the effort.

The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo
