Breaking: Working mothers face widespread discrimination in London’s commercial art world, report finds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The contemporary art world has become increasingly adept at putting feminism, gender equality and the politics of care at the centre of its public-facing programming.
  • Not far at all, according to the first ever peer-reviewed study on motherhood and discrimination in London’s commercial art world, published today by the European Journal of Cultural Studies and The Art Working Parents Alliance.
  • Industry observers note that based on a survey of 50 art world employees working across the UK capital’s galleries and auction houses, including 12 in-depth interviews, research by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi exposes a workplace culture in which mothering children often comes at considerable professional cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The contemporary art world has become increasingly adept at putting feminism, gender equality and the politics of care at the centre of its public-facing programming. Galleries mount exhibitions exploring women's experiences, champion female artists and engage with questions of representation and social justice. But how far do those values extend to the women working behind the scenes?

Not far at all, according to the first ever peer-reviewed study on motherhood and discrimination in London’s commercial art world, published today by the European Journal of Cultural Studies and The Art Working Parents Alliance.

Industry observers note that based on a survey of 50 art world employees working across the UK capital’s galleries and auction houses, including 12 in-depth interviews, research by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi exposes a workplace culture in which mothering children often comes at considerable professional cost. As the report puts it: “Becoming a parent is at the root of the glass ceiling, and for many, it represents the glass cliff.”.

It has been revealed that three-quarters of survey respondents say becoming a parent has negatively affected their career progression, while more than one in five say they had been explicitly denied promotion. One woman was told she was ineligible for promotion while on maternity leave—a breach of UK law. Just 54% received enhanced maternity pay, compared with a national workplace average of 74.1%.

It has been revealed that and these problems are not limited to smaller companies. “We assumed this would affect small art galleries with between five and 20 staff, but we found that big, multi-national galleries are also failing,” McMillan states. As the report notes: “A lack of accountability pervades the sector.”.

In a recent development, roberts-Komireddi believes that the “culture of secrecy” that enshrouds much of the art market—where financial transactions, benefits and networks are opaque and rarely disclosed—contributes to the discrimination women face when they become mothers. “Opacity really serves certain individuals and maintains this sense of fear, which was something I found particularly startling when we did our 12 in-depth interviews,” she claims. “Fear and perceived retribution pervade these workplaces and women’s relationships to these workplaces.”.

In a recent development, that fear is often felt as soon as women announce their pregnancies. The report documents, among other instances, a pregnant woman being made redundant while experiencing a high-risk pregnancy, an employer attempting to dissolve a pregnant employee’s role and use the money to hire a latest salesperson and a woman who miscarried returning to her desk immediately after a hospital appointment because she feared taking time off would damage her career. One interviewee describes feeling that by becoming pregnant she was making herself “vulnerable and less valuable”.

In a recent development, the findings also point to a deeper contradiction within an industry that publicly champions equality but often operates according to an unforgiving model of constant availability, international travel and after-hours networking. The art critic and curator Hettie Judah, who is a co-founder of The Art Working Parents Alliance, describes the colliding of 6pm private views with bedtime routines as the “witching hour” clash.

In a recent development, the difficulties are not confined to maternity leave itself. For many, the return to work can prove more damaging. Interviewees describe coming back to find their responsibilities have been redistributed, their relationships with artists and clients disrupted, or their standing within the gallery diminished. One woman discovered that a colleague who had covered her maternity leave had been given half her role, along with the artists she had spent years representing. Another returned from leave to find there was no desk for her in the gallery’s new office.

It has been revealed that crucially, the report reveals the lack of formal HR structures across the commercial art sector. Only half of the respondents worked for galleries with dedicated HR staff, while just 30 of the 50 stated their workplace had a specific maternity or parental leave policy. In some cases, employees were left to research their own entitlements, negotiate their packages and even draft policies themselves. The report’s authors say that a lack of professional HR expertise contributed to instances of discriminatory practice and breaches of the UK Equality Act.

It has been revealed that the consequences can be far-reaching. For many women, the choice has been stark: find a way to accommodate the demands of motherhood or compromise their careers. Three-quarters of the women interviewed made changes to their careers after becoming pregnant, with some moving into freelance or independent work, taking less senior positions or leaving the industry altogether. Only a third of survey respondents were offered flexible working on their return, while half were expected to be in the office four or five days a week. One interviewee described the culture as one in which “presentism is more notable than doing the work”.

Recent findings suggest that the role of class and wealth is key in shaping these experiences. The report notes how some senior figures have access to live-in nannies, au pairs and domestic help, leaving them less attuned to the financial and practical pressures facing employees who must balance childcare with demanding working hours. One interviewee stated that the management team “all had night nurses, and you know, people helping at night. So, for them to understand that you’d had three hours of interrupted sleep and were expected to be at an opening, and a dinner, get home at 12:30 and then get up at 4:30 again, was impossible”.

Sources indicate that for those on more modest salaries, the cost of childcare can make evening events and travel particularly difficult to sustain. The report suggests that the more junior and precarious the employee, the greater the likelihood of experiencing discrimination—and the fewer resources they have to challenge it.

These divisions are not simply a question of wealth, however. They also complicate assumptions about gender solidarity within an industry where women make up a significant proportion of the workforce, but senior positions are often occupied by men. As Roberts-Komireddi points out, the assumption that women will necessarily support other women can be misleading—some of the more surprising testimonies in the report describe male directors showing greater sympathy towards pregnant employees than their female counterparts.

These accounts suggest that the treatment of working mothers is shaped not simply by the gender of those in positions of authority, but by a wider workplace culture in which employees have little power to challenge established practices. Indeed, the report argues that discriminatory treatment is widespread, identifying breaches of the Equality Act in the experiences of all the women interviewed. Yet legal cases rarely make it to an employment tribunal. “In the UK, people only have three months to bring a tribunal, which is not a lot of time, particularly if you’re about to give birth,” Roberts-Komireddi says. “There’s a reluctance to go down that route because it’s a long, tiring, expensive process.”.

Looking ahead, the report’s authors hope to set best practice in the art industry. “If you look at huge corporations like Google, they have changed their policies in order to retain and attract mothers who make excellent staff—we could learn a lot from them,” Roberts-Komireddi claims.

I dare Apple to make this delightful AirPods design a reality

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I've been talking a lot lately about how Apple seems to have rediscovered its sense of fun.
  • Recent findings suggest that the iMac G3 days have become synonymous with the halcyon days of Y2K tech design.
  • A post shared by Krishnavi Anand Krishnavi (@blessed_krishnavi).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I've been talking a lot lately about how Apple seems to have rediscovered its sense of fun. From folding iPhones to touchscreen MacBooks, via an uncharacteristically zany new TikTok presence, the company is doing a lot to persuade us it's in a more playful mode of late. But if Apple really wants to convince me it's here for a good time, it needs to make these nostalgic AirPods a reality.

Recent findings suggest that the iMac G3 days have become synonymous with the halcyon days of Y2K tech design. Think bold citrus colours and translucent plastic. Those colours have made an unexpected return with the new iMac and, of course, the MacBook Neo. Apple's in-ear AirPods, however, remain available in any colour you like – as long as it's white. But wouldn't a splash of Y2K colour make them so much more fun?

A post shared by Krishnavi Anand Krishnavi (@blessed_krishnavi).

Concept artist Krishnavi Anand Krishnavi has been sharing nostalgic Apple product concepts on Instagram for a while, including an iPhone SE revival I would love to see. But it's the 'AirPods G3' that are the most fun, with their noughties design sensibilities. There's a lot going on inside an AirPod, and that colourful translucent plastic tantalisingly reveals some of its secrets.

"Apple might get me if they bring back these gems," one Instagram user comments, while another adds, "If these don’t actually come out I will sue." Another rather dispiritingly chimes in, "Apple will never do something this fun and imaginative.".

But we are seeing more imagination from Apple lately, at least when it comes to its phones and laptops. For now, though, if it's colourful AirPods you're after, you'll have to make do with the AirPods Max while waiting for the standard AirPods to go full retro. Alas, you might be waiting a while – perhaps even longer than it takes for the company to bring back the iPod.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

Frieze Abu Dhabi Debuts to Brisk Sales and Confident Dealers

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1263 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on the morning of Frieze Abu Dhabi’s inaugural edition, Saudi Arabia’s financial center in Riyadh was reportedly attacked by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
  • Frieze is bringing its A-game to Abu Dhabi, where they have the best museums,” Yantrasast told ARTnews, cheekily mentioning that he’s been putting dots on artworks from The Third Line, Taymour Grahne Projects, Experimenter and Pearl Lam Projects.
  • It has been revealed that the dealers were in high spirits too, as booths started to get busy an hour after the opening.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on the morning of Frieze Abu Dhabi’s inaugural edition, Saudi Arabia’s financial center in Riyadh was reportedly attacked by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The crowd in Abu Dhabi, at least, had other things on their minds: the fair was about to open, with millions of dollars’ worth of art ready to be sold. Members of the royal family were back after getting a sneak peek yesterday, alongside politicians and celebrities including tennis star Venus Williams and architect Kulapat Yantrasast.

“It’s about time. Frieze is bringing its A-game to Abu Dhabi, where they have the best museums,” Yantrasast told ARTnews, cheekily mentioning that he’s been putting dots on artworks from The Third Line, Taymour Grahne Projects, Experimenter and Pearl Lam Projects. Related Articles In the Shadow of War, Frieze Abu Dhabi Continues With 'Business as Usual' The Art Market Wanted to Go Global--It Didn't Plan for Everything That Means.

It has been revealed that the dealers were in high spirits too, as booths started to get busy an hour after the opening. At Thaddaeus Ropac, three of Imran Qureshi’s Water Bodies sold for $60,000, each to a UAE-based collection, though the gallery declined to specify whether this was a private or institutional collection.

“There is a great energy around the fair in Abu Dhabi this week. We’re having good conversations with collectors who are well-informed about the artists we are presenting, and you can feel the impact of the institutional scene here,” Xenia Geroulanos, director at Thaddaeus Ropac, told ARTnews.

The fair is under the umbrella of Frieze and has rebranded from Abu Dhabi Art fair, and attendees are noticing a difference. The exhibitor list has been streamlined to 89, down from 142 last year. Dealer Asmaa Al-Shabibi told ARTnews that when she walked through the fair’s upcoming entrance, it felt “a little bit like going into Frieze London, and it feels like a different fair.”.

Sources indicate that samy Ghiyati, co-founder of art advisory NG Partners, agreed. “The quality is definitely higher, and galleries made an effort to bring very good inventory. Usually fairs in the region are slower and sales happen over the course of several days,” he told ARTnews.

One of Ghiyati’s clients placed three orders on pieces ranging from $10,000 to $400,000. Within an hour of opening, dealer Sundaram Tagore had already placed two works on hold, one by Hiroshi Senju and another by Chun Kwang Young, ranging from $40,000 to $400,000. By late afternoon, Timothy Taylor had sold its entire solo presentation of paintings by Hilary Pecis to institutional and private collections in the region and internationally, to the price of $65,000-$205,000. The London-based antiquities gallery David Aaron sold a 2,000-year-old funerary stele for a seven-figure sum to a private collector, while Dubai-based Taymour Grahne Projects also sold out its booth of mosaic works depicting 70s-era architecture in Abu Dhabi.

Regional collectors reportedly spent big at Frieze Abu Dhabi. Iris Projects sold two works by Shamsa Al Omaira, a sculpture acquired by a newly introduced foundation in the UAE for $32,000 and an acrylic on canvas by Juma Al Haj for $20,400. UAE-based collectors also bought two ceramics by Eman Al Hashemi, priced at $17,000 and $15,000, an oil pastel on linen by Dhabia Al Qubaisi for $10,500, and a photograph by Ammar Al Attar for $12,500.

By then, Lawrie Shabibi had sold seven pieces by artists Hamra Abbas and Shaikha Al Mazrou, priced from $10,000 to $120,000. “People are recognizing the work when they’re coming here,” noted the gallery’s cofounder Asmaa Al-Shabibi, referring to a newly introduced client who bought a work by Al Mazrou, who has a solo exhibition at the Cultural Foundation.

Rayan Ben El Mlih, sales and marketing manager at Waddington Custot, told ARTnews that a large contingent of collectors with reserves hailed from Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Qatar and Bahrain. The gallery brought works by Etel Adnan, Sophia Vari and Fabienne Verdier.

Dealers noted that local collectors, some of whom began their collections by acquiring Western artists, are now deepening their collections with more historical pieces by regional artists.

In a recent development, “We’ve been seeing European collectors diversifying their collections, too,” said Ghiyati. Dubai’s Carbon 12 sold a painting and a sculpture by 28-year-old artist Sarah Al Mehairi, as well as two works by Mexican artist Edgar Orlaineta, priced between $17,570 and $35,000 (€16,000-€32,000).

“We’ve engaged mostly with collectors that we’ve cultivated relationships with for a while, and this is our home fair,” Judy Karkour, associate director of Carbon 12, told ARTnews.

Collectors are branching out beyond SWANA this year, with notable interest in art from the African continent and its diaspora and Latin America. Meanwhile this year’s Frieze Masters section is dedicated to trade across the Indian Ocean, taking its cues from the Louvre Abu Dhabi’s current exhibition “Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean.” An hour into the fair, Efie Gallery had placed two works by Malian artist Abdoulaye Konaté on reserve, both priced between $45,000 to $65,000, in addition to two works by Cuban artist Maria Magdalena Campos Pons ($27,500-$55,000).

Industry observers note that “Frieze Abu Dhabi has got off to a strong start for us with a high volume of enquiries in the first few hours from both institutions and private collections,” Kwame Mintah, cofounder of Efie Gallery, told ARTnews, which specializing in artists of African descent. “One of the more encouraging developments across the Gulf has been the gradual maturation of its collecting community, accompanied by a growing appreciation for artistic practices beyond established geographical and institutional frameworks,” he added.

Industry observers note that at Daniel Crouch Rare Books, a private collector bought the first map to name Abu Dhabi, dated to 1832. While dealer Daniel Crouch declined to say how much the map sold for, he priced the booth’s total value between $10,073 and $1.19 million (AED 37,000 to AED 4.4 million).

“Abu Dhabi is becoming a cultural hub in the region with a lot of development,” Crouch said. “It’s the logical place to come to for dealing in the larger Indian Ocean region and the Louvre Abu Dhabi exhibition has attracted quite a lot of attention—we’ve obviously jumped into it with alacrity.” London-based antiquities gallery ArtAncient, carrying pieces ranging from $5,000 to $5 million, sold a collection of shipwreck jewels for an undisclosed sum—the gallery also had a visit from Venus Williams, who was admiring the Graeco-Roman mummy portrait Portrait L, which had recently been dubbed the “Mona Lisa of the Middle East.”.

Sources indicate that throughout the opening, the blue-chip-leaning powerhouses, including Gagosian, Pace Gallery, Thaddaeus Ropac, and Victoria Miro, boasted crowded booths. Gagosian’s dedicated Roy Lichtenstein booth became the step and repeat for many visitors—the gallery said it “placed many” works with collectors “reputable collections” without revealing specifics.

Judging by its debut, Abu Dhabi has become a no-brainer stop on the art fair calendar. The emirate is slowly integrating into the art circuit. Earlier this month, Christie’s hosted its first fine art auction there, with Sotheby’s own version due next month, joining a colorful lineup of events that includes the Formula 1 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Finance Week and Culture Summit Abu Dhabi.

Several dealers cited the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi’s upcoming December opening with the strong pull to participate in Frieze Abu Dhabi, characterizing the museum as a bridge between West and East.

“The Guggenheim is going to open now in the next few weeks, it’s literally where contemporary art gets space to breathe and to grow,” stated Milo Gatti, fair coordinator at Galleria Continua.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Creativebloq ↗ Open Full Page

This cosy Godot-made indie game makes you feel like a still life artist

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you're looking for an antidote to the GTA 6 noise, Glenmara: Still Life Artist is it.
  • Industry observers note that despite the title, it's also not a painting game like, say, Mario Paint, but rather a simulation.
  • According to recent reports, instead, it's about being given objects you can assemble and position, then choosing filters and styles with the available tools and letting the game render it for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're looking for an antidote to the GTA 6 noise, Glenmara: Still Life Artist is it. Think of still life art, and chances are an oil painting of fruit in a bowl or flowers in a vase. While you may be presented with those options in Glenmara, this casual, cosy game from four-person Dundee-based indie studio Bit Loom Games also lets you get creatively weird with more contemporary objects and styles.

Industry observers note that despite the title, it's also not a painting game like, say, Mario Paint, but rather a simulation. "It's just this small idea based on being interested in how scenes are composed," artist Caitlin Smith tells me.

According to recent reports, instead, it's about being given objects you can assemble and position, then choosing filters and styles with the available tools and letting the game render it for you. Artist Douglas Flinders adds, "The thinking there is you are playing the role of a competent artist, so the player has access to nice painting styles. It's like you don't need to be able to triple-jump in real life to do it in Mario. You get to feel that fantasy without necessarily needing the inherent skill yourself.".

In a recent development, even though you are technically painting on a canvas, the filters you have available aren't limited to painting styles. Sure, you can use traditional oil paints or watercolours, but you can also opt for mosaic or styles that resemble cel-shading or pixel art. Being free to break from conventional expectations has been an vital design decision.

Industry observers note that "The [initial] idea was that you could be scored on how well you compose a theme with traditional rules, but it changed pretty swiftly after we realised it would just be much more fun to not have any rules and basically be able to do whatever you want creatively," Smith explains. "It was key to us to not have any sort of failed state. So if you want to sort of make this niche for yourself as a painter that puts eggs in all of your paintings, the game is not going to tell you you can't do that.".

As the team's first game made with the open-source engine Godot, which only debuted its own asset store earlier this year, all of Glenmara's shaders for its different art styles were created from scratch by programmer Henry Pullan.

It has been revealed that "Coming to Godot from Unity, the image processing pipeline we were used to just wasn't there, and we had to come up with a different way of getting all the data to and from the GPU at the right time," Pullan explains. "Fortunately, they're not real-time effects, and being able to process the image over a few frames lets us really easily experiment.".

Sources indicate that "This led to a system where we can stack effects on top of each other to create pretty different outcomes. The majority of the effects are using the library of shaders we've built up in different combinations to create a variety of effects.".

While playing as a newcomer to the fictional Scottish island of Glenmara might have you thinking of the premise of other cosy games like Animal Crossing: Newly introduced Horizons, the inspiration is closer to home for Bit Loom's members, who all grew up in small places, including one from Jersey in the Channel Islands.

"We're going for the small-knit community part of Scotland where everyone kind of knows each other," states Smith. "We tried to put this in the game in various ways, including character dialects, topics of conversation, your object collection and certain events that feature in the narrative. We hope that all of these things can work together to create a comforting, homely feel for players, and even a nostalgic one for some.".

This also means avoiding the trap of turning the game into a cosy capitalist sim where your still-life art is your side hustle, and you're incentivised to earn money from commissions to unlock more content.

"It would restrict creativity, and we just want people to go crazy and do loads of cool stuff in a painting," notes Flinders. "Also, the story we want to tell and the feeling you get throughout is a lot more about making these pieces of artwork as gifts for members of your community that you're getting to know in a latest place you've moved to. You're forming relationships with these people.".

Glenmara: Still Life Artist is coming soon to PC, and you can wishlist it on Steam.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Landing, a beloved Los Angeles gallery whose program was defined by its unique pairings of historical and contemporary artists, announced that it had closed. Its last exhibition was a one-night only solo for Maxwell Hendler staged on October 29.

According to recent reports, on the gallery’s website, founder and owner Gerard O’Brien wrote, “the Landing Gallery at 5118 W Jefferson Blvd is now closed. We are no longer programming at this location. We are deeply grateful to the artists, collectors, collaborators, and community who have been fellow participants in our engagements. It has been a privilege to champion extraordinary artists, present ambitious exhibitions, and create a space for meaningful exchange and discovery.” Related Articles Two More Vienna Galleries Close, Citing 'No New Collectors' and 'Challenging' Financial Landscape Prairie, Chicago Gallery That Put Conceptualism Ahead of Commercialism, Closes After Nearly a Decade.

It has been revealed that in an Instagram post, Gerard O’Brien put it more simply, “End of an era … 22 years of Gallery spaces in Los Angeles, Reform Galley 2004-2019 … the Landing Gallery 2012 -2026 … onwards. thank you Los Angeles❣️”.

Recent findings suggest that O’Brien founded the Landing in 2012 as an off-shoot of his design-focused Reform Gallery. “I never really thought there was a big difference,” he said of the distinction between art and design. He chose the name for its original location, a spot within Reform: “he cleared out the landing atop a short staircase in his furniture gallery and dedicated it to highlights of art, bringing in work by artists both contemporary and historical to display just above his design wares,” as a 2016 blog post by book publisher Phaidon reported.

In 2015, O’Brien decided that it was time for the Landing to grow, opening in a 2,800-square-foot gallery space on Jefferson Boulevard with a solo show for the late California artist JB Blunk.

Recent findings suggest that over the years, the Landing would become known for its pairings of historical and contemporary artists. At the time of its closing, its roster included four deceased artists (Jeremy Anderson, Richard Bowman, Leslie Kerr, and Fred Reichman) and five living contemporary artists (Yevgeniya Baras, Ryan Fenchel, Matt Phillips, Jonathan Ryan, and Amanda Valdez).

It has been revealed that the gallery was also known for regularly staging off-kilter group exhibitions, with titles like “Rat Bastard Protective Association” (2016), “The Useful and the Decorative” (2017), “Latest Iconography: Artists Raising Children” (2021), and “Consensual Ennui (2023). The first of these, “3 Women” (2016) took its name from a 1977 Robert Altman film as a way “to create a cross-generational dialogue that explores the intersections of craft and fine art, influence and homage,” per a release. It featured the work of Lenore Tawney from the 1960s and ’70s paired with textile pieces by Tanya Aguiñiga and paintings by Loie Hollowell. The exhibition marked the first time Tawney’s work had been exhibited in LA in nearly 50 years.

In an Artforum review, Erin Kimmel wrote, “The Landing’s handsome, restrained exhibition showcased the exquisite detail of [Tawney’s] works, which reward prolonged scrutiny with seemingly boundless formal revelations.”.

It has been revealed that to mark its 10th anniversary at its Jefferson Boulevard space, the Landing mounted a two-part anniversary exhibition. The first part, which opened in November 2025, focused on contemporary art and design and featured the work of Ruth Asawa, Wallace Berman, Bruce Conner, Lyne Foulkes, and Doyle Lane. The second part, which opened this past April, featured gallery artists as well as others who had exhibited there, including Brenda Goodman, Sam Jablon, and Lukas Geronimas.

Sources indicate that in a release for part one, O’Brien wrote, “10 Year brings together the feeling of the earliest days of the Landing Gallery when two years of exhibitions took place inside Reform Gallery on Melrose Avenue. Exhibiting art in a salon style in dialogue with decorative arts is how tL began.”.

It has been revealed that the Landing’s closure is the latest in an extended wave of closures that began in mid-2025. Los Angeles galleries have particularly been affected, with Murmurs, the Box, LA Louver, and Blum all shuttering, along with the LA outposts of Marian Goodman Gallery and Tanya Bonakdar.

In a recent development, in his statement on the gallery’s website, O’Brien added, “While our gallery doors have closed, our commitment to art and artists continues. Watch this space for news of future offsite exhibitions, activations, and special projects. Thank you for being part of the Landing’s ongoing narrative.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, christie’s finished out Newly introduced York’s fall auction week on Thursday evening at its Rockefeller Center salesroom, bringing in $145.9 million in a 56-lot sale of 21st-century art (after works by Jeff Koons and Ed Ruscha, estimated to sell for as much as $11 million between them, were withdrawn). Leading the sale was a $32.9 million Jean-Michel Basquiat painting that fell just shy of its low estimate.

It has been revealed that the sale included 20 works from the collection of Antonio Homem, longtime director of the storied Sonnabend Gallery, which was founded by his adoptive mother, Ileana Sonnabend. Sold to benefit their foundation, the works totaled $41.9 million. Also on offer were 10 works from the estate of beloved Fresh York philanthropist Agnes Gund, who died last year, totaling $25.7 million. Related Articles Piaget's Latest Release Is a Limited-Edition Andy Warhol Camouflage Watch A Tiny Monet With a Wild Backstory Just Fetched More Than 20 Times its Estimate at a Christie's Day Sale.

After the withdrawals, the sale was estimated to bring between $126 million and $192 million; the hammer total on the night fell considerably shy at $117.7 million. Over the two-hour sale, the house found buyers for 51 lots, for a sell-through rate of 91 percent. Works by John Currin, William Eggleston, Wade Guyton, Gerhard Richter, and Yayoi Kusama failed to sell.

Sources indicate that many prominent advisors were in the room, including Erica Barrish, Amy Cappellazzo, Ralph DeLuca, and Gabriela Palmieri, as well as well-known dealers like Marianne Boesky, Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn, and Christophe Van de Weghe. But there were a notable number of empty seats, and the atmosphere was unmistakably enervated after a long week of sales.

The sale started inauspiciously, with the first 19 lots, all from the Sonnabend collection, failing to hammer above their estimates. Bidding picked up only on the final lot of that trove, Jean Prouvé’s Table “Centrale” (“Trapèze”), petit modèle. The piece sold after five minutes of bidding between several specialists and a bidder in the room, before Sara Friedlander, Christie’s chairman of postwar and contemporary art in the Americas, nabbed it with a winning bid of $1.3 million. With fees, the total came to $1.7 million on a $700,000–$1 million estimate. But, all told, 10 of the 20 Sonnabend lots hammered below estimate. The collection hammered for $33.4 million, or $41.9 million with fees, against a pre-sale estimate of $35.25 million to $53.15 million (minus the withdrawn Koons, Wild Boy and Puppy). Not great any way you slice it.

It has been revealed that the most notable of the Sonnabend works was Andy Warhol’s 1962 painting Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), tagged at $6–$8 million. The soup cans show one of Warhol’s most iconic images and are practically synonymous with Pop art. Adrien Meyer, global head of private sales and the auctioneer at Tuesday evening’s 20th-century sale, traded bids with a bidder in the room, who nailed it down with a $7.3 million bid, translating to $9 million all in.

Sources indicate that also from the trove was Roy Lichtenstein’s Large Spool (1963). Standing nearly six feet high, the work had been off the market since the Sonnabends bought it from Leo Castelli Gallery four years after it was painted. It has hung in museums all over the world, and its sale comes amid a major Lichtenstein retrospective at Upcoming York’s Whitney Museum of American Art. Auctioneer Yu-Ge Wang tossed out a handful of absentee bids from the rostrum before Friedlander got it for her client with a $7 million bid, for a total of $8.6 million with fees. The work’s pre-sale estimate was $10 million to $15 million.

Jeff Koons’s six-foot-high sculpture Hulk (Friends), 2004–12, also from the Sonnabend collection, shows the comic-book hero with small creatures perched on his shoulders and was estimated at $3.5–$5.5 million. It hammered after only a few bids at $3.3 million, or $4.15 million with fees, to the house’s Michael Baptist. (Koons was also a seller this week, bringing seven artworks to auction at Christie’s on Tuesday night, totaling $104 million.).

Bidding improved marginally from there, but for the most part, this was a sleepy sale. Even the biggest attraction of the night, Basquiat’s much-touted painting Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), which dates to 1983 and measures seven feet square, failed to generate much excitement. Wang opened the bidding at $23 million, and for a few long moments it seemed there would be no bids. Then Ana Maria Celis, head of postwar and contemporary art, rescued the painting, beating out Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president and global chairman of 20th- and 21st-century art. It hammered at $28 million and sold for $32.9 million with the house’s fees.

According to recent reports, the hammer price was just shy of the $30–$50 million estimate. But the work, inspired by a sketch by Leonardo da Vinci, had been off the market for two decades, so the seller no doubt made a tidy profit. The painter’s auction market has famously exploded in the intervening years: every one of his paintings to sell for more than $10 million, all 83 of them, has done so since then.

Recent findings suggest that the large canvas, featuring the artist’s trademark scratchy messages and the titular sketchy heads against an orange background, had appreciated enormously since its previous trips to the block. It appeared at Sotheby’s London in 2000, when it fetched just above $400,000, within estimate, and again at the same house five years later, when it tripled in value to bring an above-estimate $1.3 million.

Vija Celmins’s 1990 painting Untitled (Ocean) was one of the few lots of the evening to generate a genuine bidding war. The painting came from the Gund estate; Gund bought it the year after it was painted. It drew bids from Joanna Szymkowiak, head of private sales; Arco Yu, a Christie’s Hong Kong specialist; and a woman bidding in the room. For four minutes, the three traded incremental bids until the room bidder won out. Still, that brought the hammer to only $5.75 million, just under the $6 million low estimate. With fees, the total came to $7.1 million.

Recent findings suggest that the 10 Gund works fared better than those from the Sonnabend collection, hammering for $20.4 million on a $16.95 million to $24.65 million pre-sale estimate. With fees, the total squeaked past the high estimate to reach $25.7 million.

There wasn’t much rhythm to the proceedings. A 1990 Gerhard Richter Abstraktes Bild painting from the estate of legendary art dealer Marian Goodman, who long represented the artist and bought the work from him that year, carried a $6 million to $8 million estimate. It failed to sell after garnering no bids. Three lots later, another Abstraktes Bild, from 1991, measuring three feet square and dominated by red, blue, and green, sparked a short contest between Friedlander and Rotter. Rotter eventually won it with a $7.6 million bid. With fees, the total came to $9.4 million. The painting’s pre-sale estimate was $7 million to $10 million.

Sources indicate that “The estimates were too high for this market,” Greenberg Rohatyn told ARTnews on her way out of the salesroom partway through the night. “We need to readjust, and the houses need to be at the forefront of managing expectations.”.

Boesky agreed that the estimates were too high. “And the energy was low,” she said on her way out. “The lots that were estimated too high were punished, and those estimated low were rewarded.”.

On a brighter note, a few records were notched: Jim Nutt ($1.1 million), Antonio Santín ($486,400), and Julia Jo ($409,600).

The Jo, a swirling, gestural abstraction of fiery oranges and yellows breaking against cool blues and teals, was the night’s final lot, estimated at $30,000–$50,000. Sold to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless, the abstraction generated arguably the most spirited bidding of the evening. Wang opened bidding at $20,000, and it promptly climbed into the hundreds of thousands as a cacophony of specialists and a bidder in the room called out bids. It eventually went to the room bidder at a hammer price of $320,000, or $403,200 with fees. That set off a hearty round of applause, at least for one lot.

In a recent development, the sale finished out an auction week that started Monday with a two-part $378.7 million Sotheby’s auction including works from cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum as well as a various-owner The Now and Contemporary sale. Christie’s staged a nearly three-hour 20th-century sale on Tuesday that totaled $626.6 million, led by a record-breaking $85.8 million abstraction by Wassily Kandinsky, closely followed by an $82.3 million landscape by Gustav Klimt. The same night, Phillips sold $104.4 million in modern and contemporary art on Tuesday, led by a $44.6 million Amedeo Modigliani sculpture. On Wednesday, Sotheby’s staged a $777.8 million Impressionist and modern art sale, led by a record-breaking $190.4 million Vincent van Gogh.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Syam Sreeshylam.

Curving ceilings sweep down to frame the two small gardens that flank this home in Kerala, India, designed by local architecture studio Fictional Project.

Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.

This led Fictional Project to pull the home’s built volume back to create space for two planted yards on either side, overlooked by the home’s pared-back and open interiors.

“The residence is careful not to overpower, becoming one with the landscape,” the studio told Dezeen.

Interstitial Living is organised around a bedroom at its centre, which is housed within a cubic volume finished in cement plaster.

A small window in this bedroom overlooks a potted tree within a cut-out in the floor of the adjacent living room, which faces the yard to the west through a row of full-height windows above a built-in timber bench.

On the opposite side of the home, the kitchen overlooks the eastern yard through a row of windows above its countertops. Both these spaces are defined by the curving white-plastered ceilings overhead, which sweep down from the centre of the home.

According to recent reports, “The scale of the residence allows for intimate working spaces in the kitchen and a welcoming living room, all accentuated by the dynamic nature of the roof. The other spaces negotiate the private/public nature of the indoors,” the studio explained.

“The concavity of the roof creates a visual connection to the outdoors, becoming a marker that emerges from within the site.”.

Sources indicate that “It breaks the rigidity of a traditional sloping roof, helping create fluid indoor spaces. Nothing here is built or conceived in isolation, but rather as interconnected systems,” it added.

The smaller first floor contains a second bedroom, bathroom and a study area, which overlook the living space below from a steel-framed landing and internal windows.

While the internal finishes were kept minimal, the exterior of the home and its boundary walls were built using terracotta-toned textured blocks, which the studio described as introducing a sense of “groundedness and warmth”.

Other dwellings in Kerala recently featured on Dezeen include a home by InLe Architects framed and shaded by two large mango trees and a farmhouse by Evolving Radical Aesthetics that is built into a hillside above a carved-out, open-air temple.

Photography by Syam Sreeshylam.

Tech Report: Adobe’s democratisation of design doesn’t have to be the death of human creativity

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A week on from my Adobe MAX 2026 experience, I'm left more conflicted than ever about the democratisation of design.
  • Recent findings suggest that add Adobe's balls to the wall AI adoption and it feels like we're snowballing into a mass slopathon.
  • According to recent reports, MAX made one thing abundantly clear – Adobe is for everyone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A week on from my Adobe MAX 2026 experience, I'm left more conflicted than ever about the democratisation of design. While post-MAX clarity has calmed the excitement of Sneaks and latest Adobe software announcements, an uncertain existentialism still lingers. Finally, everyone has the freedom to create, but in the same breath, oh dear... everyone has the freedom to create.

Recent findings suggest that add Adobe's balls to the wall AI adoption and it feels like we're snowballing into a mass slopathon. Throughout MAX, I am constantly assured AI is only there for those who want it, but I'm also hyperaware that its siren song is far too tempting for certain creatives. It all boils down to one question. In the age of democratised creativity, what defines real design?

According to recent reports, MAX made one thing abundantly clear – Adobe is for everyone. Whether you're a novice creative looking to jazz up a poster, a seasoned influencer wanting clickworthy content or an industry vet trying to adapt to the ever-demanding creative industry, Adobe is, by its own positioning, your best friend.

Industry observers note that this is where cracks already begin to form. Classically trained graphic designers, web developers and old-school content creators who learned through education or self-taught graft are left feeling cheated while newly introduced-gen creatives have it all at their fingertips. It's not childish to feel that things are a little unfair. There is value to the blood, sweat and tears of art created over time – something AI appears to extinguish.

Industry observers note that and while on the surface, creativity for everyone feels like a utopian dream, the addition of AI makes me worried. Of course, jobs are sacrificed under the guise of saving time and budget, and when everyone can create, where do we find value in creativity?

Can a concept half-baked by a computer hold the same emotional nuance as human-made work? I fall in the camp of no. But art has always been subjective – who's to say an AI-generated design has less value when, at its core, it was sparked by a human idea? A better question is, where do we draw the line?

It's easy to make Adobe the fall guy for the rise in AI slop, but it's just as much a matter of how we use its tools. At Sneaks, I witnessed a number of genuinely innovative tools, like Project Deep Brush – an AI-powered lighting-aware tool for Photoshop – that proved there's a distinct difference between full-send gen AI and the odd tool to make your everyday workflow a little smoother. Adobe developers aren't sitting in front of an evil AI cauldron preying on the downfall of human design as we know it. Behind the scenes, there are glimmers of hope.

If used in a measured way, I believe AI tools can be an extension of creativity, but with no constraint other than the moral, and Adobe churning out corner-cutting AI tools with reckless abandon, it's no surprise there's slop everywhere. Latest creatives are hungry to push the confines of what creativity can be – AI is proposed to them as a wacky friend that can do it all. The role of 'creative' is in a state of flux, and with a new generation redefining what creativity means, artistic value has never been more abstract.

Sources indicate that A repeated argument for Adobe's influx of AI innovations was the creative industry's increasing demand for content. A graphic designer may now be expected to be a master of motion design, web development and social media with fewer resources and even less time. These tools are merely a part of evolution – embrace them or get left behind.

In a recent development, but from the sidelines, I watch in horror as the creative industry eats itself over and over again. More content requires faster output. Faster output is aided by time-saving AI tools. Saved time means more space to create more content to feed the hungry attention economy. We're creating more, but as a result, we're losing a sense of quality and control. And when creativity is democratised, I worry valuable work gets lost in the shuffle.

I worry I'm a snob – that my jaded opinions are stuck in a creative world that no longer exists – but despite my discomfort, I remain hopeful. Creative democracy has its value. Accessibility is better than ever (given you can afford an Adobe subscription), and voices that may not have had the confidence to create are now empowered to do so thanks to Adobe's tools.

But what of the classic designer, like my father, who has spent decades curating their craft, only to have AI do it in seconds? It's an uncomfortable reality, but change is inevitable. To the jaded, fearful or downright nihilistic creative, I implore you to continue creating on your own terms, whether that means dipping a toe into AI tools or outright denunciation of the technology. Amidst the formulaic sea of AI, it's the quality, human-made content that will be celebrated.

Was Grandma Moses a Foil to Modernity, or a Product of It?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that grandma Moses’s landmark survey at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Arkansas opens with a flash of fire.
  • Starting with fire does prime the viewer to recognize the heat of Moses’s oeuvre, an intensity she channeled into careful, repetitive marks—tidy stacks of hay, carefully shaded leaves, the checkered grid of farm fields.
  • According to recent reports, moses was no stranger to patient work, having spent her life on farms in New York state and Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that grandma Moses’s landmark survey at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Arkansas opens with a flash of fire. A scene of a bridge burning in Troy is ablaze in red and orange; another painting, Fire in the Woods (1940), crackles with flames and smoke. This emphasis on fire, thunderstorms, and extreme weather in the first room seems to be an anticipatory rebuke to any potential complaints about Moses’s relentless good cheer. Despite a long and often sorrow-filled life—Anna Mary Robertson (“Grandma”) Moses lost five of her 10 children in infancy—Moses held fast to life’s joys in her art, and most of the paintings in the show are happy scenes of work, celebration, and family. Related Articles Sharif Bey Wins Inaugural Spector Craft Prize At The Momentary, Lucy Sparrow Transforms a Supermarket into a Felt Wonderland.

Starting with fire does prime the viewer to recognize the heat of Moses’s oeuvre, an intensity she channeled into careful, repetitive marks—tidy stacks of hay, carefully shaded leaves, the checkered grid of farm fields. Cambridge Valley (1942) is a scene of steady eye, mind, and hand, an expansive view of the Latest York countryside rendered with lovingly topographic attention. There’s almost no loss of detail as you look across the valley, a result of Moses’s unhurried care. People appear in nearly all her works, simply rendered and adding elements of humor, like a man’s hat blown off by the wind in 1948’s The Thunderstorm, a perfect “O” flush against the picture plane. The fire returns, however, in Moses’s many maple sugaring scenes, flames licking the base of large pots in which sap is boiled down. Even snow scenes are made to sparkle, radiating light through Moses’s use of glitter, a new technology she applied amply to her canvases against the advice of her dealer.

According to recent reports, moses was no stranger to patient work, having spent her life on farms in New York state and Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley. Her memory of these years provided ample subject matter for the painting she took up in her late 70s, though one of the claims of the exhibition was that Moses was making art her whole life. A fireboard from 1918 was what she called her first “large picture,” while yarn pictures from the 1930s show her capacity to work with a limited palette of solid colors. These craft activities, usually cordoned off from the realm of serious art, gave Moses a point of entry into visual representation as a way of telling her own story.

Industry observers note that spanning 101 years, from 1860 to 1961, her life story ran parallel with a century of massive transformation and the rapid emergence of a modern, industrial world. That her style and subject matter remain largely unchanged over the course of her decades-long painting career—the 80 some works in the show have more similarities than differences—suggests Moses’s indifference to the revolutions happening around her. Instead, the exhibition catalog argues, Moses was in dialog with changing notions of the elderly, the increasing representation of labor in 20th-century art, and Cold War politics that sought to export a vision of American goodness.

It has been revealed that was Grandma Moses a foil to modernity, or a product of it? While her work eschews direct portrayals of industry, she reportedly solved the compositional dilemma of capturing sprawling valleys by glimpsing a reflection in a hubcap, introducing the gleam of the automobile into what feel like entirely timeless views. Her art was held up by contemporaries as an example of the “primitive,” exhibited as the quaint musings of an aging farmwife. She seemed to give America a soul, something it appeared to be lacking in the postwar era of big capital. And yet she amassed quite a lot of capital herself, through lucrative partnerships with Hallmark among other companies. She was media-savvy, appearing on talk highlights and in documentaries, leveraging the perceived powerlessness of a little old woman to charm and disarm her critics. In the end, there’s nothing more modern than nostalgia for the lost authenticity of the countryside, an authenticity Moses returns us to in her sincerely merry paintings.

Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

📅 03 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry.
  • Recent findings suggest that the act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience.
  • Sources indicate that for many, tattoos are much more than art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

Recent findings suggest that the act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

Sources indicate that for many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

In a recent development, but here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Industry observers note that whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

In a recent development, psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

Industry observers note that however, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos indicated no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It indicates, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

📅 03 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.
  • Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal.
  • European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins indicates about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of major butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

Sources indicate that “She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins states this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins notes you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

According to recent reports, coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

  • Its sale is merely the latest chapter in af Klint’s posthumous ascent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A Hilma af Klint painting sold at a Swedish auction house on Thursday for $12.7 million with fees, setting a record for the artist, whose work does not often make it to the market. That sum is about 15 times the work’s high estimate of $800,000.

In a recent development, the painting, a 1920 abstraction called Ser III No. 5, made it to auction in a sale of modern art and design at Bukowskis in Stockholm. Prior to the auction, it had been held since 1995 by the same unnamed family, who had obtained it after af Klint’s foundation deaccessioned what Bukowski described as “a small number of works.” Related Articles In Rare Market Moment, Hilma af Klint Painting Comes to Auction in Sweden A Stunning Survey of Spirits and Séances Takes Over a Baroque Palace.

Its sale is merely the latest chapter in af Klint’s posthumous ascent. The artist, who died in 1944, was little-known until a series of well-attended museum exhibitions in the 2010s repositioned her as a pioneering figure in the history of European modernism.

Sources indicate that A Guggenheim Museum exhibition in 2018—one that shattered attendance records at the New York institution—positioned her as the inventor of abstraction. She made her paintings in response to spirits she contacted; what resulted were dazzling arrays of curlicuing lines, enigmatic shapes, and Inscrutable symbols.

Sources indicate that her foundation has generally kept her work off the market, as some of her descendants argue that she did not produce her art for commercial consumption. Yet the foundation’s position on her art and legacy has been controversial in some corners, leading certain art historians to question whether her descendants have misunderstood af Klint’s intentions.

According to recent reports, at least one art historian argued this week that the Bukowskis sale was wrong. Rachel Villari, who wrote her dissertation on af Klint, told NPR, “For me, I don’t believe that you can put a price on her work. And I believe that that makes it even more desirable to people who can afford to buy her work because what would you want more than the impossible painting that you’re not supposed to have or can’t have, right? And if it’s sold, the public won’t be able to ever see that painting or have access to it again.” (As is common with auction sales, Bukowskis did not name the buyer of the af Klint.).

It has been revealed that bukowskis treated the sale as a victory, with CEO Louise Arén saying in a statement, “It is remarkable in itself to sell an abstract work by Hilma af Klint. The exceptional final price marks a historic moment, and all of us at Bukowskis are incredibly happy and proud.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Significant disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Sources indicate that going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing complications. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Recent findings suggest that light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

In a recent development, working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

Industry observers note that the flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

It has been revealed that once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

According to recent reports, regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

📅 09 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, ah, creatine!
  • Industry observers note that creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells.
  • Recent findings suggest that although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Industry observers note that creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Recent findings suggest that although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Industry observers note that now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a major-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

In a recent development, so, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s vital to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

It has been revealed that the same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Industry observers note that some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

It has been revealed that beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

According to recent reports, if you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health complications that go beyond your hairstyle.

It has been revealed that furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Sources indicate that creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.
